18.0.s.en: 1. How great is the Creator and His power!

18.0.0.en: 1 He who lives forever created all things in general. The Lord alone will be justified. 2 He permitted no one to declare His works, 3 and who has searched out His great things? 4 Who can number the power of His greatness? And who will undertake to tell of His mercies? 5 It is not for man to take away from the wonders of the Lord, nor to add to them, nor to search them out.

18.0.1.en: There is no comparison between God, who lives forever, and man, who thinks he is great if he lives a hundred years (Ps 90:10). Even if he lived a thousand years, compared with God his years are counted as a drop of water in the sea or a grain of sand in a desert. Moreover, the offering by the heavenly and the earthly of praises and glorifications to God will not add to His glory (Eccl 3:14).

18.0.2.en: God's greatness is manifested in His care for all creation (Ps 103:13-14). While man is tender toward his neighbor or some relatives and friends (13:19), God's mercy extends over the whole human race, like a shepherd who cares for the whole flock (Isa 40:11; Ps 23:1).

18.0.3.en: v After you have eaten your fill (are satisfied), give thanks in this way:

18.0.4.en: We thank You, Holy Father, for Your holy name, which You have made to dwell in our hearts, and for the knowledge and faith and immortality which You have made known to us through Jesus Your Son. Glory to You forever.

18.0.5.en: You, O Almighty Master, created the universe for the praise of His name.

18.0.6.en: And You gave men food and drink and enjoyment so that they might give thanks to You.

18.0.7.en: But You have rewarded us with spiritual food and drink, and with eternal life, through Jesus Your Son [1].

18.0.8.en: The Didache (the Teaching of the Twelve Disciples)

18.0.9.en: He who lives forever created all things [1].

18.0.10.en: It is written in the book of Genesis (Gen 1:1): "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth," and then the book explains the details of this creation, and in all these creatures, rational and irrational, glory returns to God and greatness goes back to Him.

18.0.11.en: v Grant me, O Creator, to speak of creation and its beauty and the order of its management.

18.0.12.en: With You I begin to speak when I am amazed at Your might, how far You are exalted above those who speak...

18.0.13.en: Grant my mouth to move to glorify You, for I am not qualified for that; for You are accustomed to clothe even what is ugly with glory.

18.0.14.en: For You clothed thorns with roses, as a garment more glorious than the robes of kings.

18.0.15.en: Move speech in me, as You give the thorns beautiful roses.

18.0.16.en: By Your Spirit let my tongue utter lofty and glorious things...

18.1.0.en: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh The Lord alone will be declared righteous [2].

18.1.1.en: There is no point of comparison between God the Creator and His creation, whether heavenly or earthly, for He alone is justified, that is, the just or righteous [2].

18.2.0.en: He does not permit anyone to declare His works, for who is able to search out the greatness of His works? [3]

18.2.1.en: The first question God put to Job touches the existence of his very self, for He asks him where he was when God laid the foundations of the earth for his sake (Job 38). On the one hand, neither Job nor Adam himself had yet been created, and on the other hand God created the earth for him and his brothers before they had existence. Job was not in existence when God founded the earth, and consequently he had no ability to work with God in creation or to offer counsel or even to perceive and understand what God does for his sake. How then does he dare to complain of God's plan toward him? If Job is unable to understand the laying of the foundations of the earth, can he perceive God's plan and wisdom?

18.2.2.en: v God says: What do you say? For your sake I founded the earth with such care, so would I neglect him for whose sake I created it?... He says this to those who ask Him to give an account and an explanation of events without looking to the loftiness of His wisdom. Who prompted Me to this? Who advised Me? Who came to help Me?

18.2.3.en: St. John Chrysostom v Has the day passed? Give thanks to Him who gave us the sun for the service of our daytime work, and gives us fire to light the night and to serve our other needs in life. May the night also inspire us with what moves us to prayer.

18.2.4.en: When you look to heaven and see the beauty of the stars, pray to the Lord of all visible things, the Creator of the universe, who in wisdom made all (Ps 104:24). And when you see all nature sinking into sleep, worship Him who even without our will frees us from the pressure of continual labor, and by a short period of rest restores us again to the activity of our strength. Do not allow the whole night to be for sleep; do not allow half of your life to pass without benefit in sluggish sleep and slumber. Rather, divide the time of the night between sleep and prayer. And let your very light sleep be exercises in godliness. For our dreams during sleep are often reflections of our thoughts during the day [2].

18.2.5.en: St. Basil the Great Who can measure the greatness of His power by a number?

18.3.0.en: And who adds to this measure as he describes His mercies? [4]

18.3.1.en: The Lord asked Job: "Who hath laid the measures thereof, if thou knowest? or who hath stretched the line upon it?" (Job 38:5) He asks him: If you know, who set the measures of the earth and fixed the dimensions of the equator? Who is the architect who designed the dimensions of the earth? Who held the line [3] to measure it, determining its regions and its dimensions?

18.3.2.en: The divine discourse highlights that the earth on which man lives did not come into being by chance without planning, but behind it is the supreme Architect who laid a precise plan for its construction; it was created by the wisdom of the Creator and His surpassing power.

18.3.3.en: Modern science is still trying to discover the universe around us, so we bow before all the mysteries of creation and this greatness in silence, offering glory and praise to the Creator.

18.3.4.en: v The measures were not taken without creativity, nor did they come by chance or in a random way, but God designed it with a harmonious purpose, working as a skilled architect.

18.3.5.en: St. John Chrysostom v For the man who wants and believes, the way of his perceiving God is not difficult. If you want to behold God, contemplate the perfection of the order of the creation that He brought into being by His word, and His care for it, for He created all this for the sake of man [4].

18.4.0.en: St. Anthony the Great No one can take away from them or add to them, and there is no one who can search out the wonders of the Lord [5].

18.4.1.en: All modern inventions are in reality a reshaping or discovery of matter already existing and not an addition to the creatures of God. Likewise no one can deny that God created everything, or attribute chance to creatures.

18.4.2.en: v All things spring from God. And since creatures are many and various, they have been established and have been harmonized with the whole creation. Yet when we observe them individually we find them in harmony in their contrast, like the lyre that consists of many opposing segments. But in the end it gives a continuous tone through the segments that separate one from another.

18.4.3.en: The seeker of truth must not be deceived by the gaps that separate one segment from another, or imagine that the cause of this is due to one composer or another; rather he must trust that there is one Being who made them all to prove the skill and quality and beauty of the whole work.

18.4.4.en: Those who listen to the tone must praise the Maker and glorify Him and show their wonder at His work. At one time He presents to them a high piece and at another a soft one. Let them realize the difference between these contrasting tones. And let them realize the particular nature of some of the others, and then ask what each aims at, and the reason for the contrast.

18.4.5.en: So let us never despair of fulfilling our role in life, nor frustrate the Creator. And let us not cast away our faith in the one God who created all things that exist, nor blaspheme the Creator [5].

18.5.s.en: 2. How great is the tenderness of the Creator and Savior!

18.5.0.en: 6 When a man hath done, then he beginneth; and when he leaveth off, then he shall be doubtful. 7 What is man, and whereto serveth he? what is his good, and what is his evil? 8 The number of a man's days at the most is a hundred years. As a drop of water from the sea, and as a grain of sand, so are a few years in the day of eternity. 9 Therefore the longsuffering of the Lord was prolonged toward them, and He poured out His mercy upon them. 10 He saw and knew that their end is dreadful, 11 therefore He multiplied forgiveness. 12 The mercy of man is toward his neighbor; but the mercy of the Lord is upon all flesh. 13 He reproveth, and nurtureth, and teacheth, and bringeth again, as a shepherd his flock.

18.5.1.en: If man completes his search (into the greatness of His works), then he begins anew, and if he stops he remains perplexed [6].

18.5.2.en: God's greatness is in His eternity as in His wonderful tenderness toward all men (see Ps 136). His mercy is manifested not in abstract emotion, but He works for the good of man, rebuking him and training him and teaching him. He disciplines man!

18.5.3.en: After presenting the sources of divine knowledge for man, the son of Sirach feared that man might think he had come to know God and His mysteries through philosophies and nature and the Law, etc., and so stop searching and studying in the spirit of piety and humility. Therefore the son of Sirach affirms that when man thinks he has completed his search, it befits him to begin again and not stop, because however great his experience in study, even if he thinks himself an experienced old man who has reached a hundred years of age, can he comprehend the mysteries of the eternal, everlasting God! For his whole life is like a drop of water in the sea or a grain of sand in a vast desert!

18.5.4.en: St. Didymus the Blind sees that the wise man feels a continual need for growth. Whenever he reaches some end, he feels that this is a new beginning. Even in this life, however great the spiritual knowledge we attain, when we finish this life we feel that our knowledge is incomplete, but "we know in part" (1 Cor 13:9), and we long for perfect knowledge in eternity.

18.5.5.en: With all the satisfaction the believer finds in Christ Jesus, the more he enjoys Him, the more his longing and hunger and thirst for Him increase without ceasing. In this spirit the believer lives in continual renewal and unceasing joy, and does not suffer from a sense of boredom. Therefore St. Augustine sees that it is not permissible to stop searching for the divine mysteries in a spirit of prayer, and from longing for continual knowing of God.

18.5.6.en: v Let us search in order to discover what needs to be disclosed, and what has already been discovered. What we wish to discover is hidden so that we may search for it. And since we find that it is without limit, it remains the subject of our search. Therefore it is said: "Seek His face evermore" (Ps 105:4). For even if the seeker is satisfied with knowing new depths, what he has found makes him more able to search until he reaches a new fullness according to the growth of his capacity to receive knowledge.

18.5.7.en: Therefore it was not said "Seek His face evermore" in the same sense about other matters, where it is said: "Ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth" (2 Tim 3:7). Rather, as the Preacher says: "When a man hath done, then he beginneth" [6], when we reach that life where we are thus filled, our nature will receive its utmost possibility, for we shall reach perfection and shall not seek to increase. For all that satisfies us will be revealed to our eyes. But here we seek continually, and we do not reach the reward of the existence of what we seek at the end of our search [6].

18.5.8.en: v (The Apostle Paul) says: "Brethren, I count not myself to have apprehended: but this one thing I do, forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before, I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus. Let us therefore, as many as be perfect, be thus minded" (Phil 3:13-15).

18.5.9.en: He says that perfection in this life is to forget what is behind and to press forward toward the goal set before us. For the safe goal for the seeker is to continue in the search until he reaches what he aims at and strives for. The sound goal is the one that springs from faith. For sure faith is, in a way, the beginning of knowledge, and sure knowledge will be perfected after this life, when we see Him face to face (1 Cor 13:12).

18.6.0.en: So let this thought be in us, that we may know that being drawn toward seeking the truth is safer than the arrogance of claiming to know what we do not know. So may we search as those who find, and when we find may we count that we seem to be searching; therefore "when a man hath done, then he beginneth" (see Sir 18:6) [7].

18.7.0.en: v It was said: "Seek His face evermore," and as some say: "Ever learning, and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth" (2 Tim 3:7); but rather as another says: "When a man hath done, then he beginneth" (see Sir 18:6), until we reach that life in which we are filled, and become without (wide space), for we become perfect and do not seek progress. For what suffices us appears to us. But here we must search continually, and we do not cease examining for the fruit of what we discover [8].

18.7.1.en: St. Augustine What is man? And what is his usefulness?

18.7.2.en: What is his good? And what is his evil? [7]

18.8.0.en: Here the son of Sirach measures the greatness of man against the divine greatness, and the years of man, however long, against eternal life, and man's very works before the attributes of God... "What is his good," that is, what is all the righteousness of man worth, is it not like a filthy rag, and likewise his evil, can it harm God or nullify His plan? So let those who boast of their evil be ashamed now, for they will perish and their evil will be nullified. And let those who boast of their righteousness be humbled, for all the righteousness in them is from God [9].

18.8.1.en: The number of man's days is counted great if he reaches a hundred years [8].

18.8.2.en: But they are as a drop of water from the sea, and as a grain of sand, so are the years few in comparison with the day of eternity [9].

18.9.0.en: Therefore the Lord is longsuffering toward them, and pours out His mercy upon them [10].

18.9.1.en: Since there is no comparison between the age of man and eternal life, the Lord deals with man in his weakness with longsuffering, and pours out His mercy upon him. He desires to prepare him for the blessed eternal life.

18.10.0.en: He sees and knows their end, that it is evil, therefore He offers them complete atonement [11].

18.10.1.en: The mercy of man is for his neighbor, but the mercy of the Lord is for all flesh.

18.11.0.en: He rebukes them and trains them and teaches them like a shepherd who brings his flock back to the fold [12].

18.11.1.en: The son of Sirach prepares the ancient people of God to be open to all the nations with the coming of the Messiah, the Savior of the world; therefore he affirms: "But the mercy of the Lord is for all flesh." Truly He rebukes and disciplines, but He trains and teaches in order to bring back the whole flock!

18.11.2.en: v We all need the mercy of God, as it is written: "But the mercy of the Lord is for all flesh" (18:12). But if those men needed the mercy of God, what will man say of the rest? Tell me why He made the sun to rise on the evil and the good? If He had stopped the rain for one year, would that not have destroyed everyone? And what if He allowed the rain to flood (the earth)?... It is easy for Him to destroy things and create them anew... He who has such authority over us, and sees us sin every day, and yet has not punished us, how is this except that He bears with us by His mercy [10].

18.11.3.en: v Note that the world was founded in compassion (Wis 1:14; 11:23), and then imitate your Lord. "The mercy of man is for his neighbor, but the mercy of the Lord is for all flesh" (see Sir 18:12). How "for all flesh"? It means both sinners and the righteous, for we all need mercy. We all enjoy it...

18.11.4.en: What does this blessed man say? "But I obtained mercy, because I did it ignorantly" (1 Tim 1:13). What then, does he no longer need mercy afterward? Hear what he says: "I laboured more abundantly than they all: yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me" (1 Cor 15:10). And of Epaphroditus he says: "For indeed he was sick nigh unto death: but God had mercy on him; and not on him only, but on me also, lest I should have sorrow upon sorrow" (Phil 2:27). And also: "We were pressed out of measure, above strength, insomuch that we despaired even of life: but we had the sentence of death in ourselves, that we should not trust in ourselves, but in God which raiseth the dead: who delivered us from so great a death, and doth deliver" (2 Cor 1:8-10) [11].

18.12.0.en: St. John Chrysostom He has mercy on those who receive His discipline, and who hasten to His judgments [13].

18.12.1.en: v There is nothing that the Lord hates (Wis 11:25). Surely He hates nothing, and that thing remains in existence... Certainly it does not happen that He does not will that something exist and at the same time it exists... And if He hates nothing of what He created, then He loves what He created... But He loves man with a great love that surpasses everything, since man is the noblest of the living beings He created [12].

18.12.2.en: St. Clement of Alexandria v The world is preserved by divine providence, for there is no place that this providence does not reach.

18.12.3.en: And divine providence is the carrying out of the promises of the divine Word, who gives form to the matter from which this world is composed, and He is the architect and artist of all this. For things could not have taken their beauty were it not for the prudence of the power of the Word, who is the image of God (the Father) and His mind and wisdom and providence [13].

18.13.s.en: 3. The kind word accompanies the gift

18.13.0.en: 14 He has mercy on those who receive His discipline, and who hasten to act by His judgments. 15 My son, blemish not your good deeds, neither use uncomfortable words when you give anything. 16 Shall not the dew assuage the heat? so is a word better than a gift. 17 Lo, is not a word better than a gift? but both are with a gracious man. 18 The reproach of a fool is hateful, and the gift of the envious wearies the eyes. 19 Before judgment be sure of the truth, and before speaking learn. 20 Before sickness seek healing, and before judgment examine yourself, and you shall receive pardon in the hour of visitation.

18.13.1.en: We have previously spoken about giving, how it must be accompanied by tenderness and kindness in dealing with the needy. A word, for the needy, is better than the gift; for the gift, however great its worth, loses its value if accompanied by a harsh word or look from the giver. The kind word descends on the heart of the needy like dew that cools the scorching heat, or the heat of want and need!

18.13.2.en: The Holy One is the Judge of the universe; He came not merely to offer gifts, but gave Himself, and gives us His Holy Spirit, and brings us into the Father's embrace, so that we may realize the divine love and delight in His gifts. So it befits us to walk in the same spirit!

18.13.3.en: My son, do not bring shame upon the good work you do, and do not cause grief by your words when you give a gift [14].

18.13.4.en: A man may think that he is imitating God, and stretches out his hand to give, but in truth he spoils the gift with a harsh word he directs to the needy. The pious, kind man offers the comforting word accompanying the fitting gift [14].

18.13.5.en: Does not the dew calm the heat?

18.14.0.en: So is the word better than the gift? [15]

18.14.1.en: v Father Agathon was going one day to the city to sell the work of his hands, and met a cripple on the road, paralyzed in his legs, and he asked him: "Where are you going?" He answered him: "To the city." He said to him: "Do a kindness and carry me there," so he carried him to the city. And the cripple said to him: "Set me down where you sell your work." He did so. And when he sold something, the cripple asked him: "For how much did you sell it?" He told him the price. He said to him: "Buy me a cake." He bought it for him. And when Abba Agathon sold something else, the sick man asked him: "For how much did you sell it?" He told him its price. He said to him: "Buy me this." He bought it. And when Abba Agathon had sold all his goods and wanted to go back, the cripple said to him: "Do a kindness and take me back to the place where you found me," so he carried him and returned him to it. And then the cripple said: "O Agathon, you are filled with divine blessings in heaven and on earth." And when the saint lifted his eyes he saw no man, for it was an angel whom the Lord had sent to test him [14].

18.14.2.en: The Paradise of the Fathers Truly, is not the word better than a fitting gift?

18.15.0.en: And both are found in the kind man [16].

18.15.1.en: As Sirach urges his disciples to be prudent, he requires of them self-control, especially in speech [16-19]. The wise man should be characterized by tenderness and humility along with practicing repentance for sin. This is achieved if man keeps in mind the divine judgment which every man faces [22, 24, 25].

18.15.2.en: The harsh word troubles the one to whom you gave a good gift, so that he counts what you gave him as nothing, whereas the good word is like the dew that cools the intensity of the heat (rage). Therefore man counts the good word coming from a sincere and pure heart better than material gifts.

18.15.3.en: Whoever wants to rebuke a person for a particular mistake or some sin does not choose the time at which he offers a gift to the person, because the harsh word spoils the value of the gift (and offering the gift during the advice spoils it). There is a time for the gift and a time for rebuke, in a manner befitting the one he rebukes.

18.15.4.en: v Do not make light of this wonderful benefit you enjoy through hospitality, but day by day strive to acquire for yourselves the gain of this wonderful trade, knowing that our Lord looks to the generosity of the spirit, not to the offering of large quantities of food, nor the offering of a rich table, but the offering of cheerfulness, not by words alone but also by love from the heart and a sincere mind. Therefore a certain wise man said: "Do you not see that a word is better than a good gift" (see Sir 18:16).

18.15.5.en: In many cases you have seen that attention to the word helped the needy person to return on his feet rejoicing more than the gift. Take note of this, and do not find it hard to meet visitors; instead, we on the one hand are in the position of those who relieve their poverty, doing this with love and cheerfulness, not as one who gives something but who gives a benefit of the utmost greatness. And on the other hand, if we cannot do that, let us not be impolite to them, but offer at least attention in word, responding to their troubles [15].

18.15.6.en: St. John Chrysostom v No one can say: "I am poor, I have no way of showing mercy." If you are unable to give like the rich who cast into the treasury, give two mites like the widow, and God will count this greater than the offerings of the rich (Mk 12:41-44; Lk 21:1-4).

18.15.7.en: Do you not have even this? You still have the power to show mercy, and with this power you practice mercy in serving the sick. Can you not do this? You can comfort your brother with words. By this be merciful to him with your words, and listen to him who says: "A word is better than a gift" [16].

18.15.8.en: Suppose you cannot practice mercy with words. Even so, if your brother is in an uproar against you, you can show him mercy and support him in the midst of his agitation, considering that the common enemy (the devil) is mistreating him, and instead of answering him with a harsh word and increasing his confusion, be silent and be gentle with him and with yourself, that you may snatch it away from the hand of the enemy.

18.15.9.en: Even if the brother returns to agitation against you again, you can be gentle with him and pardon his sin against you so that you may enjoy forgiveness from God. In truth God says: "Forgive, and ye shall be forgiven" (Lk 6:37), and by this you find help and mercy for your brother's soul by pardoning his sins against you [16].

18.16.0.en: Father Dorotheus of Gaza v If someone is compelled to beg alms because of hunger, and because of his begging is forced to walk in shame, and because of his shame bears disgrace, then under the weight of dejection he feels a complication accompanied by a darkness that descends on his soul. It befits the one who cares for such people to be longsuffering, and not to behave in a way that increases their dejection and provocation. It also befits him to lighten by encouragement his nature marked by dejection [17].

18.16.1.en: St. John Chrysostom The fool insults the other and shames him, and the gift of the envious man darkens the eyes [17].

18.16.2.en: The foolish man does not know how to be gentle in order to win others with tenderness and wisdom, but criticizes continually in a spirit of violence and harshness, and so crushes the souls of those he deals with.

18.16.3.en: As for the envious man, although he offers gifts to his brothers, he lacks sincere love, so he does not desire their success and progress because of his hidden selfishness; these gifts darken the eyes of others, as they do not perceive what is in his thoughts and what is in his heart of envy, as they also darken his own eyes, so he thinks that he has performed his duty in the fullest way by offering gifts without reforming his heart.

18.17.0.en: St. Jerome [18] sees that the Latin word for the envious is invidus, which came in Greek with more force, meaning one who casts a sorcerer's spell, spellcaster. The envious man is harmed by the success and progress of others. If through the envy of the devil death entered the world, he does not cease to instill the spirit of envy in man, not for the benefit of what he acquires, but to stir up his hatred against the successful.

18.17.1.en: Before you speak learn, and before you become ill take care of your health [18].

18.18.0.en: And before you judge examine yourself faithfully, and you will find atonement in the hour of visitation [19].

18.18.1.en: As man cares for his bodily health, especially when he suffers from illness, it befits him to prepare himself for eternal glory, that he may enjoy complete pardon in the day of the Lord's visitation [19].

18.19.0.en: 21 Before sickness be humble, and in the time of sins show your repentance. 22 Let nothing hinder you from paying your vow in due time, and do not hold back from works of righteousness until death, for the reward of the Lord remains forever. 23 Before you pray, prepare yourself, and do not be as one that tempteth the Lord. 24 Remember the wrath in the days of the end, and the time of vengeance when He turns away His face. 25 In the time of fullness remember the time of hunger, and in the days of wealth remember poverty and need. 26 From morning until evening the time is changed, and all things are quick to change before the Lord. 27 The wise man is wary in all things, and in the days of sins he guards against offenses. 28 Every man of understanding knows wisdom, and confesses to him that finds her. 29 Those who are of understanding in sayings complete their works with wisdom, and pour forth sound proverbs.

18.19.1.en: Before you are sick, be humble, and when you commit sins, prove your return (to God) [20].

18.19.2.en: v Whoever loves earthly things and their lusts does not think of being with Christ after his departure, and cannot say: "I am a stranger in the earth," for he is concerned with what is of the earth. But whoever says "Hide not thy commandments from me" is a saint... Therefore the prophet asks God to reveal to him the greatness of His commandments for the heavenly life [19].

18.19.3.en: Origen Let nothing prevent you from fulfilling your vow without delay, and do not wait for death to be righteous [21].

18.19.4.en: The psalmist says: "Praise waiteth for thee, O God, in Sion: and unto thee shall the vow be performed" (Ps 65:1); "Vow, and pay unto the Lord your God: let all that be round about him bring presents unto him that ought to be feared" (Ps 76:11). What does paying the vow mean but offering the sacrifice of praise and thanksgiving with joyful obedience to the beloved commandment of God!

18.19.5.en: v "Unto thee shall the vow be performed" (Ps 65:1) in Jerusalem. For we shall be there perfect, that is, we shall be perfect in the resurrection of the righteous. There all our vow will be paid, not only with respect to the soul but the body also, no longer corruptible, for it will no longer be in Babylon, but will now become a heavenly body and be changed...

18.19.6.en: Peace will prevail, and war will end. And when peace prevails, that city called the vision of peace (Jerusalem) will prevail. There will no longer be a struggle with death. But now, how grave is the death with which we struggle!

18.19.7.en: v Do not delay in the vow, for you will pay the vows not by your own strength. You will fail if you depend on yourselves. But if you depend on Him to whom you vow, you will be secure and pay the vows. "Vow, and pay unto the Lord your God." What must we all vow? To believe in Him, and hope from Him for eternal life, and live in godliness according to the measure befitting all men [20].

18.19.8.en: St. Augustine v What do we vow and pay, brethren? Believe in Him, hope from Him for eternal life and for the good life according to the common level. There is a common level for all men. "Thou shalt not commit adultery" is a commandment for the married as for the unmarried... Therefore all of us must vow what concerns faith and justice and chastity or mercy, and by the help of Him to whom we vow this we pay...

18.19.9.en: Some vow that they will not permit themselves or desire to know anyone in the future, even if they are presently unmarried. Their vow is greater than the former. Others vow this virginity from the beginning of their life, so that they never practice, unlike those who tried but afterward abandoned it; these are the greatest of all [21].

18.20.0.en: Father Caesarius, Bishop of Arles Before you vow, prepare yourself, and be not as one that tempteth the Lord [22].

18.20.1.en: Man should not tempt the Lord in his prayers and vows in choosing a particular way, nor hasten in vowing (Judg 11:29-40).

18.21.0.en: Remember His wrath in the day of your death, and in the time of punishment when the Lord turns away His face [23].

18.21.1.en: It befits us to ask God for counsel and grace that we may walk according to His good pleasure until the last breath, and hate what He hates.

18.21.2.en: v Hate hypocrisy, and everything that does not please the Lord. Do not forsake the commandments of the Lord, but keep what you have received, without adding or taking away. Confess your transgressions in the Church, and do not come to your prayer with an evil conscience. This is the way of life [22].

18.22.0.en: The Didache In the time of fullness remember the time of hunger, and in the days of wealth remember poverty and need [24].

18.22.1.en: It befits the believer in the time of his fullness to remember God's gifts to him, but while using wealth for his satisfaction, to remember the hungry!

18.22.2.en: v Since we see that God does not allow us to be swallowed up in the flood of those troubles when they come upon us, may we not allow ourselves to become careless when they pass. Let us remember that when we were sorrowful He comforted us. Let us thank Him now that we are rejoicing. In our sufferings He gave us rest and did not leave us. May we not betray ourselves in the time of ease by turning aside to laziness. One says: "In the time of fullness do not forget the time of hunger" (see Sir 18:24). Therefore let us think in the time of trial of the day of relief. And with regard to our sins let us act in the same way. If you have sinned and received forgiveness, give thanks, but do not forget the sin, not in order to goad yourself by thinking of it, but to teach yourself not to be negligent, and relapse again into the same snares (Heb 6:4) [23].

18.23.0.en: St. John Chrysostom From morning to evening the time is changed, and all things pass quickly in the presence of the Lord [25].

18.23.1.en: v You do not know what any day will bring you: "Between morning and evening the weather changes." In another place we are advised with a useful commandment: "Let us walk while we have the light, lest darkness overtake us" (see Jn 12:35).

18.23.2.en: The negligent person says: When I become old I will resort to the remedy of repentance. This wretched one does not know that when a person grows accustomed to committing sins while waiting for repentance, he will not be qualified to obtain the fruit of repentance, or will be qualified for it with difficulty [24].

18.23.3.en: Father Caesarius, Bishop of Arles v Here the times are riding on wheels to pass on, and through them wealth and poverty are distributed daily.

18.23.4.en: Whoever is rich today perhaps tomorrow will become poor, and the one who is poor now perhaps will soon become rich?

18.23.5.en: The sick man is healed, and the one who is healthy becomes sick, for this world and its activities are woven upon changes.

18.23.6.en: The child grows up, and the man grows old, and the old man dies, for there is no stature complete without change in the world.

18.23.7.en: The morning has passed, and noon comes, and the sunset draws near, and evening comes, and takes its place.

18.23.8.en: The day is delightful and its sight is loved and its beauty radiant, and the night walks in and enters in its stead and spoils it [25].

18.24.0.en: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh The wise man has the fear of God in all that he does, and in the days of sins he guards against offenses [26].

18.24.1.en: v The fear of the Lord is the bridle that stops man's rush toward committing evil, and draws him backward when he is enslaved to running after his hateful lusts, not only in his outward life but especially in his hidden inner life [26].

18.25.0.en: v The man who lives in remembrance of God at all times is filled with fear, so that even when he resists a thought of lust passing over his soul, he becomes terrified because of this thought. But the thought flees at once before the fear of the soul, like a bird that flees before the man who disturbs its rest. Fear and respect for the laws of men preserve the body against lusts. And fear and man's shame before God preserve the soul against evil thoughts. For since he knows that God sees him at all times, he watches himself continually lest he sin [27].

18.25.1.en: St. Mar Philoxenus Every intelligent man knows wisdom, and praises him who finds her [27].

18.25.2.en: The wise man says: "Happy is the man that findeth wisdom, and the man that getteth understanding" (Prov 3:13). It befits the intelligent believer to seek wisdom and be diligent in searching for it and ask the Lord to acquire it, and to praise everyone who acquires it, for it gives the blessed life, and also presents to him true and lasting riches and glory.

18.25.3.en: St. Chrysostom asks: Was St. Peter poor, that he had nothing to give to the lame man? Origen sees that the wisdom we acquire is the Law of the Lord, and it is more precious than gold and silver.

18.25.4.en: v This means: The law that proceeds from Your mouth is better for me; which is Christ. I disdain the pieces of gold and shining silver, that I may take delight in the law of Your mouth and enjoy it.

18.26.0.en: We can say that "the law of the mouth" is the order of the words that proceed from the mouth of God: the first words were spoken to beginners, while the following words were spoken to those who had received the first, until they reach perfection [28].

18.26.1.en: Origen The wise in words make others wise, and rain down sound proverbs [28].

18.26.2.en: As man strives to be wise, let him realize that God grants him wisdom when he strives by his prayers and conduct that his brothers may enjoy wisdom from God, for what he desires for his brothers in earnestness opens the door for him and for them.

18.27.0.en: 30 Do not go after your lusts, but refrain yourself from your appetites. 31 For if you give your soul the desires that please her, she will make you a laughingstock to your enemies. 32 Take not pleasure in many banquets, neither bind yourself to the expense thereof. 33 Make not yourself poor with banquets, spending upon them from borrowing, when there is nothing in your purse; for thereby you lie in wait for your own life.

18.27.1.en: St. Basil likens the soul to the horseman who knows how to tame his horse and lead it, so that he and the horse are safe. But if the horseman is inexperienced, by his wrong leading he causes harm and destruction to himself and the horse.

18.27.2.en: v The souls that are not bridled by reason, nor dominated by the mind, which suppresses their passions of pleasures and pains, and manages and directs them (soundly), these souls perish like the dumb animals. For their minds are drawn by the passions, as unruly horses draw their drivers [29].

18.27.3.en: St. Anthony the Great v Look now, beloved, at what I say: know that just as a horse is good only with respect to its swiftness in the service assigned to it, but needs a trainer who rides it and turns it to the place he wants, because the beast alone does not know what ought to be done. And just as, if the horse is ridden, it must use the things natural to it, I mean to leap and jump, so if its rider manages the causes of its movements well, the harm disappears and the benefit is obtained.

18.27.4.en: And just as it is not enough for the rider to manage the horse only, but also to acquire knowledge and habit of staying on it, then thereby the need and safety of the rider and the ridden are fulfilled. But if he does not manage it well, and is not knowledgeable and accustomed to staying on it, the horse in many instances turns aside from the straight way... and goes out into steep, rugged roads, and stumbles and falls, with its rider, and both of them come into distress. And the cause of all that is the negligence of its rider, either because he did not know how to train it, nor was accustomed to staying on it, or because he neglected its governance and management and returning it to the straight way.

18.27.5.en: So also by this example God created man, and placed in him a mind with which he reasons, in honor of the soul He created with the body. So if the soul manages well, and exercises the work of leadership as it ought, and bridles the movements of the body, it is saved and saves the body from falling into distress. But if it is negligent, and does not manage the movements of the body as it should, and is heedless and lazy and lets go of the bridle of the body, then because it has no thought, it goes out into the rugged roads and the soul falls with it into these evils. This is not because of an evil in the body - God forbid - but because the soul did not manage it as it ought [30].

18.28.0.en: v The light of the body is the eye, and the insight of the soul is the mind created in it by nature, and I do not say that the mind is other than the soul as though they were separate from each other. No, but the soul and the mind are bound by union. For the mind is a natural power of the soul. It is its inward parts, created with it, not foreign to it nor having entered it after a time [31].

18.28.1.en: v If the soul moves toward its rational faculty which is the mind (that which the Holy Trinity, Creator of all things, made implanted in it from the time He formed it), and the mind thinks of what is fitting and proper to God, then the soul becomes saved, and flees from all uses of the passions.

18.29.0.en: And when the soul goes first and observes the movements of the body and controls them, then it is in a calm and piety befitting it. And if it comes into virtuous sights according to its nature, it remains contemplating all the works of God and His glory with fear and calm, without anxiety. Rather at times you find it in amazement, looking before it to the Trinity, thinking of the glory of the divinity which cannot be comprehended because of the greatness of its light. And it remains contemplating that blessed light and wisdom without end and absence of disturbance. So if the soul keeps its mind vigilant according to its nature, and thinks of what it should, the mind must be in theoria (contemplation) of the glorified works and all that is of peace [32].

18.29.1.en: St. Basil the Great Do not follow your passions, but restrain your lusts [29].

18.29.2.en: In speaking of self-control, he warns us against deviating toward lusts and passions and a life of luxury. He also requires us to be prudent in facing material responsibilities.

18.29.3.en: v If those who are compelled by necessity to cross wide seas, when they are alert, preserve their lives, for even if the waves are raging while their boats sail, they save themselves by holding on to anything on the shore. But if they are drunk, even if they make countless attempts to swim to the shore, the wine overcomes them, and they drown amid the waves and depart from life.

18.30.0.en: So also the soul, if it falls among raging waves in the midst of the whirlpool of the currents of life, by its own striving cannot overcome the love of the body, just as it is unable to know (by itself) that it is a divine, immortal soul bound to a material, mortal body full of lusts... and that this is the touchstone for testing it, so if it allows itself to be defiled by bodily lusts, it perishes, and its perishing and going out of the circle of salvation is the result of its negligence and its drunkenness with ignorance and its contempt for goodness. The body is like a river which often swallows us up with base pleasures [33].

18.30.1.en: v Sin finds help for itself in matter, and the body becomes a throne for it. But the rational soul, when it understands this, casts off from itself the burden of matter, and rises from under its weight, and perceives God Almighty, and washes the body carefully without entrusting it, since it is an enemy and adversary to it. By this God crowns the soul, as it overcomes the lusts and evils [34].

18.30.2.en: v The free man is the one whom (bodily) pleasures do not enslave, but who controls the body with good discernment and chastity, content with what God gives, however little, thanking Him with all his heart.
